sources.title: Alabama Football Defensive Line Depth Suffers Major Injury Blow
sources.text: Alabama head coach Kalen DeBoer unlikely to close on elite WR Monshun Sales. Getty Alabama football has suffered another significant injury setback heading into the 2026 season. According to a report from Yea Alabama, Crimson Tide defensive lineman Jeremiah Beaman will miss the entire 2026 season after suffering a torn ACL in his left knee during practice Sunday. Beaman underwent surgery Tuesday, with Dr. Lyle Cain performing the procedure at UAB St. Vincent’s. The injury is a major blow to Alabama’s defensive line depth just days before the start of the regular season. Jeremiah Beaman Suffers Season-Ending ACL Injury Beaman’s injury was initially reported after Alabama head coach Kalen DeBoer confirmed Monday that the third-year defensive lineman had been injured during practice. The Crimson Tide was awaiting further testing at the time before providing additional details. Those tests confirmed the worst-case scenario. Beaman suffered a torn left ACL and will now miss the entire 2026 season. The Birmingham native entered the 2026 season looking to establish himself as an important piece of Alabama’s defensive front. The 6-foot-4, 301-pound defensive lineman is a former Parker High School standout and is entering his third year with the Crimson Tide. This is particularly difficult news for Beaman, who was already coming off a season-ending ACL injury suffered during the 2025 season. He started Alabama’s 2025 opener against Florida State before suffering the injury in practice the following week. Now, Beaman will be forced to miss another full season because of the same type of injury. Alabama Will Need Its Defensive Line Depth Injuries are an unavoidable part of college football, but losing a player like Beaman this close to the start of the season is particularly difficult. Alabama will now have to rely on the depth it has developed throughout the offseason. The Crimson Tide has invested heavily in building its defensive line, and that depth could prove extremely important in the coming weeks. With Beaman officially out for the season, younger players and veterans alike will have opportunities to earn additional snaps. Alabama will need those players to step up. The Crimson Tide’s defensive line has already been an area worth monitoring throughout fall camp. Now, Beaman’s injury adds another layer of uncertainty to the position heading into the 2026 season. For Beaman, the priority is much simpler: begin the long road back. The Alabama defensive lineman has already overcome one ACL injury. Now he faces another difficult rehabilitation process. The Crimson Tide will certainly miss him in 2026. Like HEAVY's content? Be sure to follow us . knownOutputs.bodyMarkdown:
Jeremiah Beaman's second Alabama season ended before it began.

Kalen DeBoer confirmed Monday that Beaman injured his knee during Sunday practice. Further testing found a torn ACL in his left knee, and Beaman underwent surgery Tuesday at UAB St. Vincent’s with Dr. Lyle Cain performing the procedure. He is expected to miss the entire 2026 season.

The Birmingham native is 6-foot-4 and 301 pounds. He started Alabama’s 2025 opener against Florida State, then suffered a season-ending ACL injury in practice the following week. This is now his second season-ending ACL injury in two years.

That timeline matters because Beaman never got the ordinary stretch of Saturdays that turns a young defensive lineman into a dependable part of a rotation. Alabama had already seen enough to start him in an opener. It has not seen enough of him over a full season to know what his workload, stamina, and late-season role would have become.

## The defensive line has lost more than one name

A 301-pound lineman affects how a defense parcels out snaps. He can occupy space inside, absorb double teams, and allow the rest of the front to play with fresher legs. Beaman's absence does not automatically tell Alabama who replaces him. It tells the staff that one expected part of the weekly distribution is gone before the first game.

The available reporting does not identify a confirmed replacement or provide a new depth chart. That matters. Naming a substitute now would turn an open roster question into a fact that has not been established.

Alabama will have to decide whether the answer comes from a player already prepared for a larger role, a different combination of bodies, or a rotation that changes from opponent to opponent. Those choices will show up in ordinary downs before they show up in any season summary. Who handles first and second down inside. Who remains available when the game reaches the fourth quarter. Who can stay on the field without forcing the defense to protect the replacement.

## Two injuries have changed the evaluation

Beaman's first ACL injury came after he started the Florida State opener in 2025. The new injury came during Sunday practice, before he could build on that return. The football cost is immediate, but the evaluation problem is longer lasting.

Alabama now has to judge its defensive line without the player who was supposed to supply evidence about his own development. Coaches cannot evaluate how Beaman would have handled a full schedule, how his snaps might have changed against different fronts, or whether his 2025 starting role would have expanded. Those answers are unavailable because the season is unavailable to him.

That is a difficult roster problem without making it a verdict on the entire defense. Alabama still has time before September to establish the order behind him. It simply has less time to experiment with the expectation that Beaman would stabilize part of the rotation.

## Alabama’s early practices now carry more weight

The next useful information will come from personnel decisions, not broad assurances. A new starter would show that one player has earned the staff’s trust quickly. A deeper rotation would show Alabama prefers to divide Beaman’s work rather than hand it to one replacement. Neither choice should be treated as settled until the program identifies it.

Beaman’s absence also makes communication between the defensive line and the linebackers more important. A front can survive one missing body more easily when the remaining players know their assignments, play with consistent pad level, and avoid creating clean running lanes while chasing fresh pass-rush snaps. Those details are not visible in a preseason roster graphic. They appear when the offense runs the same concept twice and the defense handles it correctly the second time.

The staff does not need a dramatic answer. It needs a group that can make the same decision repeatedly, through the opening month, without asking one unproven player to solve every down Beaman would have played.

Alabama’s defensive line will be judged by how well it distributes Beaman’s missing snaps before anyone can judge the replacement by name.

By Alabama’s September 2026 opener, the depth chart and the first rotation should show whether the unit found a dependable way to divide that work. That is the grading point for this piece.
